story.e:
Jacob was very old now, and one day he fell ill. Someone told Joseph: *Your father is sick.* Joseph took his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, and brought them to his old father. Manasseh was the older one, and Ephraim was the younger.

Jacob gathered his strength and sat up in bed. He said: *Your two sons will be mine, just like my own sons.* In other words, he took his two grandsons as his own sons. That way they too would share in what God had promised the family.

Then Jacob said: *Bring them to me, so that I may bless them!* To bless means to ask God for good things for someone, and to say it out loud. Jacob's eyes were weak, and he could hardly see. He hugged the boys and kissed them.

Joseph placed his sons so that the older one, Manasseh, was next to Jacob's right hand. In those days the right hand meant the stronger, bigger blessing, and it usually went to the older son. But Jacob crossed his hands! He put his right hand on the head of the younger boy, Ephraim, and his left hand on Manasseh.

Then he blessed them: *May God, who has been my shepherd all my life, bless these boys!* A shepherd watches over his sheep, leads them and protects them. Jacob's life had many hard times, but he could see that God had looked after him all along, the way a shepherd looks after a lamb.

Joseph noticed the crossed hands, and he did not like it. He wanted to fix it: *Not like that, father! This one is the firstborn. Put your right hand on him!* But Jacob would not let him. He said: *I know, my son, I know. He too will be great. But the younger will be greater than he is.* Jacob himself had been a younger brother, and he knew: God does not choose by our rules.

Jacob also told Joseph: *I am about to die, but God will be with you and will bring you back to the land where your fathers lived.* That was the land of Canaan.

At last Jacob called all twelve of his sons together: *Gather around, so that I can tell you what will happen to you!* He spoke to each one in turn. Not everything he said was pleasant. He even spoke about the wrong that Reuben, the oldest, had done. The truth can be spoken with love.

About Judah he said: *The royal scepter will not depart from Judah.* A scepter is a fancy staff that kings hold in their hands. It meant that kings would come from Judah's family. Many, many years later King David was born into Judah's family, and the last book of the Bible, Revelation, cries out: *The Lion of the tribe of Judah has triumphed!* Judah had once done something very wrong, yet he received the greatest promise.

He compared Joseph to a fruitful tree, full of fruit, with branches climbing over the wall. Joseph's life had brought much good to others.

When Jacob had blessed all twelve of his sons, each with the blessing meant for him, he finished what he wanted to say. He lay back on his bed and died in peace.
story.m:
When Jacob fell ill, Joseph brought his two sons, Manasseh and Ephraim, to see him. Jacob sat up in bed and first spoke about the most important experience of his life: *God Almighty appeared to me at Luz in the land of Canaan, and there he blessed me.* God had promised him many descendants and the land. Then he went on: *Your two sons, born to you in Egypt before I came here, will be mine. Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.* He adopted his two grandsons as his own sons, so they would share in the promise just the same. You can become part of God's family through being welcomed in.

Jacob asked: *Who are these?* Joseph answered: *They are the sons God has given me here.* Jacob's eyes were dim, but he kissed them and embraced them: *I never expected to see your face again, and now God has let me see your children too.*

Joseph led the boys forward so that Manasseh, the firstborn, stood at Jacob's right hand. The right hand meant the stronger blessing. But Jacob crossed his arms: he put his right hand on Ephraim, the younger, and his left on Manasseh. Then he blessed them: *May the God before whom my fathers Abraham and Isaac walked, the God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day, the angel who has redeemed me from all harm, bless these boys!*

Joseph was displeased and tried to move his father's hand: *Not so, my father! This one is the firstborn.* Jacob refused: *I know, my son, I know. He too will become a people, and he too will be great, but his younger brother will be greater than he.* God's leading mattered more than custom, and Jacob understood this from his own life: his experience became a help to others. Then he said: *I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.* He looked back over his life, saw that God had been his shepherd, blessed his sons and grandsons, and pointed ahead to the future. Faith does not live only in the present.

After this he called all his sons: *Gather around, so that I can tell you what will happen to you in the days to come!* The blessings were not all alike; each son received the one meant for him. Reuben, the firstborn, lost his rank because he had dishonored his father's bed: rank does not protect us from the consequences of our own choices. Simeon and Levi were warned because of their anger, since they had treated others cruelly: *Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce!* He would scatter them in Israel. But of Judah he said: *Judah, your brothers will praise you. You are a young lion. The scepter will not depart from Judah until he comes to whom it belongs.* He compared Joseph to a fruitful vine whose branches climb over the wall. Archers attacked him, but his bow stayed steady, because the Mighty One of Jacob held him up. A faithful life bears fruit for others too.

Finally Jacob asked them to bury him with his fathers in the cave of Machpelah in Canaan. When he had finished what he had to say, he drew his feet up into the bed and died. A life at peace can come to a peaceful end. What God has done for us, we too can tell the next generation.

**What the Bible does not say:** It does not tell us how Jacob, with his weak eyes, knew which boy was which. One word in the saying about Judah (*Shiloh*) has an uncertain meaning, so it is translated in different ways. The Bible recalls Simeon and Levi's old violence, and Jacob condemns it, but it does not describe it again. Nor does it tell us how the sons received their blessings.

If someone at home is old or ill, or you have lost someone and it weighs on you, talk to an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher, or a pastor.
story.h:
Two chapters, and both say the same thing: blessing does not follow our rules. Jacob's crossed hands are not a mistake or an old man's confusion: he knows exactly what he is doing. The text says *he crossed his hands on purpose* (the Hebrew *sikkel et-yadav* means he arranged his hands wisely, deliberately). All his life he had been learning this: he himself was the younger son whom God chose. Before he was born it was said: *the older will serve the younger* (Genesis 25:23). His father Isaac, too, was the younger one, chosen instead of Ishmael. The pattern goes on: Isaac, not Ishmael; Jacob, not Esau; Ephraim, not Manasseh. God's choice does not follow human order. Custom does not decide the order; blessing is God's free decision, not a human entitlement.

The scene is carefully built. Jacob does not begin with his illness but with the fact that God appeared to him at Luz, that is, Bethel. Then he adopts the two grandsons as his own, *as Reuben and Simeon*, so they will become two tribes, and Joseph receives a double share. He also mentions Rachel, who died on the road at Ephrath, near Bethlehem. When Joseph tries to move his hand, Jacob answers in a few words: *I know, my son, I know.* That sentence holds the experience of a whole life. It is the same situation as when Jacob himself tricked the blind Isaac out of a blessing. Now Jacob is the one who cannot see, but no one deceives him: he knows better.

And notice how he names God in the blessing: *the God who has been my shepherd all my life*. The Hebrew *ha-ro'eh oti* literally means: the one who has shepherded me. These words come from Jacob, a shepherd himself, who cheated his brother, fled from home, served a deceitful master for twenty years, lost his wife, and mourned his son for twenty-two years. Even so he says: he has been my shepherd. Looking back, he sees that God was with him all along. Faith is not denying the hardships but recognizing God within them. In chapter 49 he says it again: *the Shepherd, the Rock of Israel*. What we know about God must be passed on, and that is exactly what Jacob does here with the next generation.

The blessings in chapter 49 are not flattering: Jacob names his sons' sins as well. Reuben is *turbulent as the waters*, and he loses the birthright because he went up to his father's bed. Simeon and Levi's swords are weapons of violence; Jacob is pointing to the bloodshed at Shechem: *Cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel.* Blessing is not keeping quiet about faults but speaking the truth about the future: you can name reality and still give someone a future. Many blessings play on the names, because the text itself builds them that way: *Judah, your brothers will praise you* (*Yehudah, attah yodukha*); *Dan will judge his people* (*Dan yadin*); *Gad will be attacked by raiders* (*Gad gedud yegudennu*). Joseph is *a fruitful vine* (*ben porat*), which echoes *parah*, to bear fruit, the word the Bible uses to explain Ephraim's name. Among the sons Jacob also slips in a short prayer: *I wait for your salvation, O LORD.*

The other sons' blessings are shorter, but they too are built from pictures. Zebulun lives by the seashore, Issachar is a strong donkey bending under its load, Naphtali is a doe set free, Asher's bread is rich, and Benjamin is a ravenous wolf. These pictures describe the later home and character of the tribes more than the sons themselves. At the end of chapter 48 Jacob also gives Joseph a special gift: *one ridge of land* (Hebrew *shekhem*, which is also the name of the town of Shechem), which he took *with my sword and my bow*. That short sentence also points to the land God had promised.

And the greatest promise goes not to Joseph, the successful son, but to Judah. Judah's road was long: he sold a brother for money, took responsibility for Benjamin, then offered to take his brother's place as a slave, and now he receives the royal promise. *The scepter will not depart from Judah, nor the staff from between his feet, until he comes to whom it belongs, and the obedience of the nations is his.* The Hebrew word here is *Shiloh*, and its meaning is debated: it may mean *the one to whom it belongs* (part of the ancient translations read it so), it may be a place name (Shiloh), or it may mean *tribute to him*. Every reading points to a ruler yet to come. Why Judah? Because he learned to stand firm, and God's grace is greater than the past. The sentence points a thousand years ahead: to the kingdom of David, who came from the tribe of Judah, and in Christian reading to Jesus, born in Bethlehem of Judah. The book of Revelation quotes this promise: *Do not weep! Behold, the Lion of the tribe of Judah, the Root of David, has triumphed* (Revelation 5:5). There the promise about Judah reaches its fullness, and its lion imagery begins right here, at Jacob's bedside.

Jacob's last words about the land do not revolve around himself: *I am about to die, but God will be with you and bring you back to the land of your fathers.* His faith reaches beyond his own life: God will bring the people back. He also gives exact instructions for his burial: he asks to be laid in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah lie, and where he buried Leah. Then *he finished instructing his sons*, drew his feet up into the bed, breathed his last, and *was gathered to his people*. In the Bible that phrase is the language of a peaceful death.

**What the Bible does not say:** It does not settle what *Shiloh* means exactly; translators and interpreters still debate it, and we do not settle it either. It does not tell us whether the blessings are predictions in every detail or rather a father's words that later echoed in the history of the tribes. We do not know how Manasseh felt when his younger brother was put ahead of him. The Bible does not soften what Reuben, Simeon and Levi did; Scripture tells even about its heroes what they did wrong, and here Jacob names the wrong too. It reports the violence but does not call it right.

If someone at home is old or ill, or your family is grieving and it weighs on you, talk to an adult you trust: a parent, a teacher, or a pastor.

verse.text: The God who has been my shepherd all my life to this day.

story.e:
Amikor Jákób meghalt, József az édesapja fölé hajolt, megcsókolta őt, és sírt. Nagyon szerette az apját. Egész Egyiptom hetven napig gyászolta Jákóbot, vagyis szomorú volt miatta.

Aztán József nagy kísérettel felvitte az édesapját Kánaánba, ahogy Jákób kérte. A makpélai barlangban temették el, ahol Ábrahám és Izsák is nyugodott.

Amikor visszatértek Egyiptomba, a testvérek újra megijedtek. Azt gondolták: *Mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk azért, amit tettünk?* Üzenetet küldtek neki, aztán odamentek hozzá, leborultak előtte, és ezt mondták: *A szolgáid vagyunk.*

József sírva fakadt, amikor ezt hallotta. Nem akarta, hogy féljenek tőle. Így válaszolt: *Ne féljetek! Isten helyében vagyok én? Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította, hogy sok ember életben maradjon.* Megígérte nekik: *Gondoskodom rólatok és a gyermekeitekről.* Kedvesen beszélt velük, és megnyugtatta őket.

József száztíz évig élt. Még az unokái gyermekeit is látta. Amikor a halála közeledett, így szólt a testvéreihez: *Isten biztosan gondot visel rátok, és felvisz erről a földről arra a földre, amit megígért. Vigyétek magatokkal a csontjaimat!*
story.m:
Jákób meghalt, és József az édesapja fölé hajolt, megcsókolta őt, és sírt. Egyiptom is gyászolt: hetven napig siratták az öreg embert, mert a király főemberének édesapja volt. Egy hitből élő élet messzire elér, még idegen országban is.

József ezután engedélyt kért a fáraótól, nem titokban ment, hanem szabályosan. Ezt mondta: *Az apám megesketett, hogy abban a sírban temessem el, amelyet ő készített magának Kánaánban.* A fáraó beleegyezett. Nagy kíséret indult el, szekerek, lovasok és egyiptomi főemberek is a testvérekkel együtt. A gyerekek és a nyájak otthon maradtak Gósenben. Így jutottak el Kánaánba, ahol Jákóbot a makpélai barlangban temették el, Ábrahám és Izsák sírja mellé.

A temetés után visszatértek Egyiptomba, és a testvéreket utolérte a régi félelem. Az édesapjuk halála hozta vissza. Egyetlen dolog tartotta vissza Józsefet, gondolták, a tisztelet az apjuk iránt, és most ő már nincs. *Mi lesz, ha József most mégis megfizet nekünk mindazért, amit tettünk vele?* Először üzenetet küldtek neki, aztán személyesen is odamentek, leborultak előtte, és azt mondták: A szolgáid vagyunk. A gyógyulás nem egyetlen pillanat; a félelem néha akkor is visszatér, amikor már mindent rendezettnek hittünk.

József sírva fakadt, amikor az üzenetet meghallotta. Nem haragudott, hanem megszólalt: Ne féljetek! Isten helyében vagyok én? Nem akart bíró lenni; azt, hogy mi lesz a testvérei sorsa, nem ő dönti el. Aztán kimondta a bűnt is, nem szépítette: *Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította, hogy sok ember életben maradjon.* A megbocsátás nem a valóság elfedése.

Megígérte: *Ne féljetek: gondoskodom rólatok és a gyermekeitekről.* Így megvigasztalta őket, és kedvesen beszélt velük.

József száztíz évig élt, és még az unokái gyermekeit is látta. Egész életét idegen földön, Egyiptomban élte le, mégis hűségben. Isten áldása nemzedékeken át folytatódott: a hetven emberből, akik annak idején lementek Egyiptomba, nagy nép lett. Amikor közeledett a halála, megkérte a testvéreit: *Isten biztosan gondot visel rátok, és felvisz erről a földről arra a földre, amelyet az őseinknek megígért. Vigyétek majd magatokkal a csontjaimat!* Meg is esküdtek rá. József meghalt, és Egyiptomban koporsóba helyezték.

A csontok sorsa az Exodusban folytatódik: Mózes valóban magával vitte őket, amikor mintegy négyszáz év múlva Izráel kivonult. Végül a Sikem melletti földön temették el. Isten emlékezett az ígéretére akkor is, ha évszázadok teltek el. A Zsidókhoz írt levél ezt a hit jeleként említi József életéből.
story.h: Mózes első könyve egy koporsóval ér véget Egyiptomban – és mégis ez a könyv egyik legreménytelibb lapja. Két mondat áll a középpontjában. Az első: *Isten helyében vagyok én?* József ezzel adja vissza a bírói szerepet annak, akit illet. Hatalma lett volna megfizetni, de nem vállalja el Isten helyét. Aki ezt megérti, az szabadul fel a bosszú kényszere alól. A második mondat az egész József-történet összefoglalása: *Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.* Figyeljük meg, mit nem mond. Nem azt, hogy nem is volt rossz. Nem azt, hogy úgysem fájt. Nem azt, hogy végül is minden jól alakult, hagyjuk. Kimondja a bűnt, és kimondja Isten munkáját is – a kettő nem zárja ki egymást. Ez a bibliai megbocsátás: nem letagadás, hanem átadás. És figyeljük meg azt is, hogy a testvérek félelme huszonkét év után sem múlt el teljesen: az apjuk halálával újra előjött. Ezért kell József másodszor is kimondania ugyanazt. A megbocsátást néha többször kell elfogadni, mint ahányszor kimondják. A könyv utolsó kérése pedig egy hitvallás: *Vigyétek magatokkal a csontjaimat.* József egész Egyiptomot kormányozta, de tudta, hogy nem Egyiptom az otthona. Négyszáz évvel később Mózes valóban magával vitte a csontjait, és végül az ígéret földjén helyezték nyugalomra. A könyv tehát nem véget ér, hanem nyitva marad – és így adja át a történetet Mózesnek.

verse.text: Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.

e.q: Mit tett József, amikor az édesapja meghalt?
e.qe: What did Joseph do when his father died?
oe: He bent over him, kissed him and wept
He went straight to the palace

v.t: József az apja fölé hajolt, megcsókolta őt, és sírt.

ve.t: Then Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.

e.q: Meddig gyászolta Egyiptom Jákóbot?
e.qe: How long did Egypt mourn Jacob?

v.t: Egyiptom hetven napig gyászolta Jákóbot.

ve.t: And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.

e.q: Hol temették el Jákóbot?
e.qe: Where was Jacob buried?
oe: In Canaan, in the cave at Machpelah
On the bank of the Nile

v.t: Jákóbot a makpélai barlangban temették el, Ábrahám sírja mellé.

ve.t: They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre, which Abraham had purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site.

e.q: Kik nyugodtak még abban a barlangban?
e.qe: Who else rested in that cave?

v.t: Ott temették el Ábrahámot és feleségét, Sárát, ott temették el Izsákot és feleségét, Rebekát, és ott temettem el Leát is.

ve.t: There Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried, and there I buried Leah.

e.q: Mitől féltek a testvérek a temetés után?
e.qe: What were the brothers afraid of after the funeral?
oe: That Joseph would now pay them back
That there would be no grain
That they would have to go home
That Pharaoh would drive them out

v.t: A testvérek megijedtek: mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk?

ve.t: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge?”

e.q: Mit mondtak a testvérek Józsefnek?
e.qe: What did the brothers say to Joseph?

v.t: A testvérek leborultak előtte: a szolgáid vagyunk.

ve.t: His brothers also came to him, bowed down before him, and said, “We are your slaves!”

e.q: Mit tett József, amikor ezt meghallotta?
e.qe: What did Joseph do when he heard this?

v.t: József sírt, amikor ezt az üzenetet hallotta.

ve.t: When their message came to him, Joseph wept.

e.q: Mit kérdezett József a testvérektől?
e.qe: What did Joseph ask the brothers?

v.t: Ne féljetek! Isten helyében vagyok én?

ve.t: Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?

e.q: Mit mondott József arról, amit a testvérei tettek?
e.qe: What did Joseph say about what his brothers had done?
o: „Ti rosszat terveztetek, de Isten jóra fordította.”
oe: “You planned evil, but God turned it to good.”

v.t: Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.

ve.t: What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

e.q: Mit kért József a halála előtt?
e.qe: What did Joseph ask before he died?
oe: That they carry his bones with them
That they stay in Egypt for ever
That they build him a statue

v.t: Vigyétek magatokkal a csontjaimat! – kérte József.

ve.t: And then you must carry my bones up from this place.

m.q: Miért gyászolta Egyiptom is Jákóbot?
m.qe: Why did Egypt mourn Jacob too?
o: Mert a király főemberének édesapja volt
oe: Because he was the father of the king’s chief official

v.t: Egyiptom hetven napig gyászolta Jákóbot.

ve.t: And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.

m.q: Mit kért József a fáraótól?
m.qe: What did Joseph ask of Pharaoh?
o: Engedélyt, hogy Kánaánban temesse el az apját
oe: Permission to bury his father in Canaan

v.t: „Apám megesketett engem: temess el abban a sírban, amelyet Kánaán földjén készítettem magamnak. Engedd meg, hogy elmenjek, és eltemessem apámat, azután visszatérek.”

ve.t: My father made me swear an oath when he said, I am about to die. You must bury me in the tomb that I dug for myself in the land of Canaan.’ Now let me go and bury my father, and then return.

m.q: Kik mentek el a temetésre?
m.qe: Who went to the funeral?
oe: A great company, with Egyptian officials

v.t: Nagy kísérettel mentek fel Kánaánba a temetésre.

ve.t: Joseph went to bury his father, and all the servants of Pharaoh accompanied him … Chariots and horsemen alike went up with him, and it was an exceedingly large procession.

m.q: Mi hozta vissza a testvérek félelmét?
m.qe: What brought the brothers’ fear back?

v.t: A testvérek megijedtek: mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk?

ve.t: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge?”

m.q: Hogyan közelítették meg Józsefet a testvérek?
m.qe: How did the brothers approach Joseph?
oe: They sent a message, then bowed before him

v.t: A testvérek leborultak előtte: a szolgáid vagyunk.

ve.t: His brothers also came to him, bowed down before him, and said, “We are your slaves!”

m.q: Mit ígért meg József a testvéreknek?
m.qe: What did Joseph promise the brothers?
o: Hogy gondoskodik róluk és a gyermekeikről
oe: That he would provide for them and their children
That he would send them back to Canaan
That he would make them all rulers
That he would forget their names

v.t: Ne féljetek! Gondoskodom rólatok és a gyermekeitekről.

ve.t: Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.

m.q: Hogyan beszélt József a testvéreivel a végén?
m.qe: How did Joseph speak with his brothers at the end?
o: Megvigasztalta őket, és kedvesen beszélt velük
oe: He comforted them and spoke kindly
He did not speak with them again

v.t: Ne féljetek! Gondoskodom rólatok és a gyermekeitekről.

ve.t: Therefore do not be afraid. I will provide for you and your little ones.

m.q: Hány évet élt József?
m.qe: How many years did Joseph live?

v.t: József és apjának háza népe Egyiptomban maradt; József száztíz évig élt.

ve.t: Now Joseph and his father’s household remained in Egypt, and Joseph lived to the age of 110.

m.q: Kiket látott még meg József az élete végén?
m.qe: Whom did Joseph still see at the end of his life?

v.t: Látta az unokáit és azok gyermekeit is.

ve.t: He saw Ephraim’s sons to the third generation, and indeed the sons of Machir son of Manasseh were brought up on Joseph’s knees.

m.q: Mit mondott József Istenről a halála előtt?
m.qe: What did Joseph say about God before he died?
o: „Isten biztosan gondot visel rátok, és felvisz erről a földről.”
oe: “God will surely take care of you and bring you up out of this land.”

v.t: Isten biztosan gondot visel rátok, és felvisz erről a földről.

ve.t: But God will surely visit you and bring you up from this land to the land He promised on oath to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.

h.q: Mivel ér véget Mózes első könyve?
h.qe: How does the book of Genesis end?

v.t: József száztíz éves korában meghalt. Bebalzsamozták, és Egyiptomban koporsóba helyezték.

ve.t: So Joseph died at the age of 110. And they embalmed his body and placed it in a coffin in Egypt.

h.q: Mit ad vissza József a kérdéssel: „Isten helyében vagyok én?”
h.qe: What does Joseph hand back with the question “Am I in God’s place?”
o: A bírói szerepet annak, akit illet
oe: The judge’s role to the one it belongs to

v.t: Ne féljetek! Isten helyében vagyok én?

ve.t: Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?

h.q: Mi szabadít fel a bosszú kényszere alól?
h.qe: What sets a person free from the compulsion of revenge?
o: Ha nem vállaljuk el Isten helyét

v.t: Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.

ve.t: What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

h.q: Mit NEM mond József a „jóra fordította” mondatban?
h.qe: What does Joseph NOT say in the “turned it to good” sentence?
o: Hogy nem is volt rossz, amit tettek
oe: That what they did was not evil
That God turned it to good

v.t: Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.

ve.t: What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

h.q: Mi a bibliai megbocsátás lényege e szerint a fejezet szerint?
h.qe: What is the heart of biblical forgiveness according to this chapter?

v.t: Ti rosszat terveztetek ellenem, de Isten jóra fordította.

ve.t: What you intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.

h.q: Miért kellett Józsefnek másodszor is kimondania ugyanazt?
h.qe: Why did Joseph have to say the same thing a second time?
o: A testvérek félelme újra előjött az apjuk halálával
oe: The brothers’ fear came back when their father died
He had forgotten what he said
The brothers had not heard it the first time

v.t: A testvérek megijedtek: mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk?

ve.t: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge?”

h.q: Mit tanít az, hogy a megbocsátást többször kell elfogadni?
h.qe: What do we learn from forgiveness needing to be accepted more than once?
o: A szív lassabban hisz, mint ahogy a szó elhangzik
oe: The heart believes more slowly than the words are spoken
It is better not to say it at all

v.t: A testvérek megijedtek: mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk?

ve.t: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge?”

h.q: Mi a hitvallás József utolsó kérésében?
h.qe: What is the confession of faith in Joseph’s last request?
o: Tudta, hogy nem Egyiptom a nép otthona
oe: He knew Egypt was not the people’s home
He did not trust his brothers

v.t: József hitte, hogy a nép kimegy Egyiptomból, ezért rendelkezett a csontjairól.

ve.t: By faith Joseph, when his end was near, spoke about the exodus of the Israelites and gave instructions about his bones.

h.q: Mi történt később József csontjaival?
h.qe: What happened later to Joseph’s bones?
o: Mózes magával vitte, és Sikemben temették el
oe: Moses carried them, and they were buried at Shechem
They stayed in Egypt for ever
They were lost in the desert

v.t: Mózes magával vitte József csontjait, ahogy megígérték.

ve.t: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.”

h.q: Miért nem zárul le igazán Mózes első könyve?
h.qe: Why does the first book of Moses (Genesis) not really close?
o: Nyitva marad, és átadja a történetet Mózesnek
oe: It stays open and hands the story on to Moses
Because the last chapter was lost

v.t: Mózes magával vitte József csontjait, ahogy megígérték.

ve.t: Moses took the bones of Joseph with him because Joseph had made the sons of Israel swear a solemn oath when he said, “God will surely attend to you, and then you must carry my bones with you from this place.”

e.q: József nem sírt, amikor az édesapja meghalt.
e.qe: Joseph did not weep when his father died.

v.t: József az apja fölé hajolt, megcsókolta őt, és sírt.

ve.t: Then Joseph fell upon his father’s face, wept over him, and kissed him.

e.q: Egyiptom hét napig gyászolta Jákóbot.
e.qe: Egypt mourned Jacob for seven days.

v.t: Egyiptom hetven napig gyászolta Jákóbot.

ve.t: And the Egyptians mourned for him seventy days.

e.q: Jákóbot Egyiptomban temették el.
e.qe: Jacob was buried in Egypt.

v.t: Jákóbot a makpélai barlangban temették el, Ábrahám sírja mellé.

ve.t: They carried him to the land of Canaan and buried him in the cave at Machpelah in the field near Mamre, which Abraham had purchased from Ephron the Hittite as a burial site.

e.q: Jákóbot abba a barlangba temették, ahol Ábrahám és Izsák is nyugodott.
e.qe: Jacob was buried in the cave where Abraham and Isaac also rested.

v.t: Ott temették el Ábrahámot és feleségét, Sárát, ott temették el Izsákot és feleségét, Rebekát, és ott temettem el Leát is.

ve.t: There Abraham and his wife Sarah are buried, there Isaac and his wife Rebekah are buried, and there I buried Leah.

e.q: A testvérek megijedtek, hogy József most megfizet nekik.
e.qe: The brothers were afraid Joseph would now pay them back.

v.t: A testvérek megijedtek: mi lesz, ha József most megfizet nekünk?

ve.t: When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “What if Joseph bears a grudge?”

e.q: József megbüntette a testvéreit.
e.qe: Joseph punished his brothers.

v.t: Ne féljetek! Isten helyében vagyok én?

ve.t: Do not be afraid. Am I in the place of God?

e.q: József azt kérdezte: „Isten helyében vagyok én?”
e.qe: Joseph asked: “Am I in God’s place?”

story.e:
When Jacob died, Joseph bent over his father, kissed him and wept. He loved his father very much. All Egypt mourned Jacob for seventy days, which means the people were sad for him.

Then Joseph went up to Canaan with a great company and took his father there, as Jacob had asked. They buried him in the cave of Machpelah, where Abraham and Isaac also rested.

When they came back to Egypt, the brothers became afraid again. They thought: *What if Joseph pays us back now for what we did?* They sent him a message, and then they went to him, bowed down before him and said: *We are your servants.*

Joseph burst into tears when he heard this. He did not want them to be afraid of him. He answered: *Do not be afraid! Am I in God’s place? You planned evil against me, but God turned it to good, so that many people would stay alive.* He promised them: *I will provide for you and your children.* He spoke kindly to them and comforted them.

Joseph lived a hundred and ten years. He even saw his grandchildren’s children. When his death was near, he said to his brothers: *God will surely take care of you and bring you up out of this land to the land he promised. Carry my bones with you!*
story.m:
Jacob died, and Joseph bent over his father, kissed him and wept. Egypt mourned too: they wept for the old man for seventy days, because he was the father of the king's chief official. A life lived in faith reaches far, even in a foreign country.

Joseph then asked Pharaoh for permission. He did not go secretly but in the proper way. He said: *My father made me swear to bury him in the tomb he dug for himself in Canaan.* Pharaoh agreed. A great procession set out, with chariots, horsemen and Egyptian officials going along with the brothers. The children and the flocks stayed behind in Goshen. So they reached Canaan, where Jacob was buried in the cave of Machpelah, next to the tombs of Abraham and Isaac.

After the burial they returned to Egypt, and the old fear caught up with the brothers. It was their father's death that brought it back. They thought that only one thing had held Joseph back, respect for their father, and now he was gone. *What if Joseph still holds a grudge and pays us back for all we did to him?* First they sent him a message, then they went to him in person, bowed down before him and said: We are your servants. Healing is not a single moment; fear can come back even when we thought everything was settled.

Joseph wept when he heard the message. He was not angry. He said: Do not be afraid! Am I in the place of God? He did not want to be the judge; what would become of his brothers was not for him to decide. Then he named the wrong too, without softening it: *You planned evil against me, but God turned it to good, so that many people would stay alive.* Forgiveness does not cover up the truth.

He promised: *Do not be afraid. I will take care of you and your children.* So he comforted them and spoke kindly to them.

Joseph lived to be one hundred and ten, and he even saw his grandchildren's children. He spent most of his life in a foreign land, Egypt, yet he lived it faithfully. God's blessing went on from generation to generation: the seventy people who had once gone down to Egypt had become a great nation. As his death drew near, he asked his brothers: *God will surely take care of you and bring you up out of this land to the land he promised our ancestors. Carry my bones with you when you go.* They swore to do it. Joseph died, and in Egypt he was placed in a coffin.

The story of the bones continues in Exodus: Moses did carry them along when Israel left Egypt about four hundred years later. In the end they were buried in the land near Shechem. God remembered his promise even when centuries went by. The letter to the Hebrews names this as a sign of faith in Joseph's life.
story.h: Genesis ends with a coffin in Egypt — and yet this is one of the most hopeful pages in the book. Two sentences stand at its centre. The first: *Am I in God’s place?* With this Joseph hands the judge’s role back to the one it belongs to. He had the power to pay them back, but he will not take God’s place. Whoever understands this is set free from the compulsion of revenge. The second sentence sums up the whole Joseph story: *You planned evil against me, but God turned it to good.* Notice what he does not say. Not that it was not evil. Not that it did not hurt. Not that it all worked out in the end, so let it go. He names the sin, and he names God’s work as well — the two do not cancel each other out. This is biblical forgiveness: not denial, but handing over. Notice too that the brothers’ fear had not entirely passed even after twenty-two years: their father’s death brought it back. That is why Joseph must say the same thing a second time. Forgiveness sometimes has to be accepted more often than it is spoken. And the book’s last request is a confession of faith: *Carry my bones with you.* Joseph governed the whole of Egypt, but he knew Egypt was not his home. Four hundred years later Moses really did carry his bones, and in the end they were laid to rest in the promised land. So the book does not come to an end — it stays open, and hands the story on to Moses.

bio.hu: Az első ember, akit Isten a föld porából formált, és az élet leheletét lehelte belé. Ő adott nevet az állatoknak, és ő őrizte az Éden kertjét.
bio.en: The first man, formed by God from the dust of the ground and given the breath of life. He named the animals and kept the Garden of Eden.

en.q: Whom did Adam name?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Ádám a föld porából lett, és Isten élet leheletét lehelte belé.

en.q: True or false: Adam was made from the dust and God breathed the breath of life into him.

hu.q: Mit mondott Ádám, amikor meglátta Évát?
o: Csont az én csontomból, test az én testemből

en.q: What did Adam say when he saw Eve?
o: Bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh

hu.q: Kire fogta Ádám a bűnét?

en.q: Whom did Adam blame for his sin?

hu.q: Hány évet élt Ádám?

en.q: How many years did Adam live?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Ádám visszatérhetett az Édenbe.

en.q: True or false: Adam could return to Eden.

bio.hu: Az első asszony, akit Isten Ádám oldalbordájából alkotott. Neve azt jelenti: minden élők anyja. A kígyó őt csábította el először, de Isten neki is ígéretet adott a Szabadítóról.
bio.en: The first woman, made by God from Adam's rib. Her name means mother of all living. The serpent tempted her first, but God gave her too the promise of the Saviour.

hu.q: Miből alkotta Isten Évát?

en.q: From what did God make Eve?

hu.q: Mit jelent az Éva név?

en.q: What does the name Eve mean?

hu.q: Ki beszélt Évával a tiltott fáról?

en.q: Who spoke to Eve about the forbidden tree?

hu.q: Mit mondott Isten: mi nem jó az embernek?

en.q: What did God say is not good for man?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Éva adott a gyümölcsből Ádámnak is.

en.q: True or false: Eve gave some of the fruit to Adam too.

hu.q: Kire fogta Éva a bűnét?

en.q: Whom did Eve blame?

hu.q: Mit ígért Isten Éva utódjáról?

en.q: What did God promise about Eve's offspring?
o: He will crush the serpent's head

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Évát Isten a föld porából formálta.

en.q: True or false: God formed Eve from the dust of the ground.

bio.hu: Ádám és Éva második fia, juhpásztor. Nyája legjavából, hittel vitt áldozatot Istennek, aki kedvesen tekintett rá. Testvére, Káin irigységből megölte – ő az első vértanú.
bio.en: The second son of Adam and Eve, a shepherd. He offered the best of his flock to God in faith, and God looked on him with favour. His brother Cain killed him out of envy – the first martyr.

hu.q: Mi volt Ábel foglalkozása?

en.q: What was Abel's occupation?

hu.q: Mit vitt Ábel áldozatul?

en.q: What did Abel bring as an offering?

hu.q: Kinek az áldozatára tekintett az Úr?

en.q: Whose offering did the Lord look upon with favour?

hu.q: Ki volt Ábel testvére?

en.q: Who was Abel's brother?

hu.q: Hol halt meg Ábel?

en.q: Where did Abel die?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Ábel hittel vitte áldozatát a Zsidókhoz írt levél szerint.

en.q: True or false: According to Hebrews, Abel offered by faith.

hu.q: Mi kiáltott Istenhez a földből?

en.q: What cried out to God from the ground?

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Ábel volt Ádám és Éva elsőszülött fia.

en.q: True or false: Abel was the firstborn son of Adam and Eve.

bio.hu: Igaz ember volt, aki Istennel járt. Engedelmesen megépítette a bárkát, és Isten megmentette őt és családját az özönvízből. Vele kötötte Isten a szivárvány-szövetséget.
bio.en: A righteous man who walked with God. He obediently built the ark, and God saved him and his family from the flood. God made the rainbow covenant with him.

hu.q: Milyen ember volt Noé?

en.q: What kind of man was Noah?

hu.q: Kik voltak Noé fiai?

en.q: Who were Noah's sons?

hu.q: Milyen fából épült a bárka?

en.q: What wood was the ark built from?

hu.q: Hány ember menekült meg a bárkában?

en.q: How many people were saved in the ark?

hu.q: Hány napig esett az eső?

en.q: How many days did it rain?

hu.q: Melyik madár hozott olajfalevelet Noénak?

en.q: Which bird brought Noah an olive leaf?

hu.q: Mi lett a szövetség jele Noéval?

en.q: What was the sign of the covenant with Noah?

hu.q: Mit tett Noé, miután kilépett a bárkából?

en.q: What did Noah do after leaving the ark?
o: He built an altar and sacrificed

hu.q: Igaz vagy hamis: Noé maga zárta be a bárka ajtaját.

en.q: True or false: Noah shut the ark's door himself.

hu.q: Hány éves volt Noé, amikor az özönvíz jött?

en.q: How old was Noah when the flood came?

bio.hu: Isten elhívta Úr városából, és megígérte neki, hogy nagy néppé lesz, és benne nyer áldást a föld minden nemzetsége. Hitt Istennek, és útra indult, pedig nem tudta, hová megy.
bio.en: God called him out of the city of Ur and promised that he would become a great nation, and that all the families of the earth would be blessed through him. He believed God and set out, not knowing where he was going.

hu.q: Melyik városból hívta el Isten Ábrahámot?

en.q: From which city did God call Abraham?

hu.q: Mit ígért Isten Ábrahámnak?
o: Hogy nagy néppé lesz, és benne áldást nyer minden nemzetség

en.q: What did God promise Abraham?
o: That he would become a great nation and a blessing to all families
That he would be king of Egypt
That he would never have to travel
That he would be a rich merchant

hu.q: Mi volt Ábrahám feleségének a neve?

en.q: What was the name of Abraham's wife?

hu.q: Mihez hasonlította Isten Ábrahám utódainak számát?

en.q: To what did God compare the number of Abraham's descendants?
o: To the stars of the sky
To the stones of the mountains
To the fish of the river
To the leaves of the trees

hu.q: Hogyan indult el Ábrahám, amikor Isten elhívta?
o: Hitt Istennek, pedig nem tudta, hová megy

en.q: How did Abraham set out when God called him?
o: He trusted God, not knowing where he was going

hu.q: Mi volt Ábrahám fiának a neve, akit az ígéret szerint kapott?

en.q: What was the name of the son Abraham received according to the promise?

hu.q: Melyik földre vezette Isten Ábrahámot?

en.q: To which land did God lead Abraham?

hu.q: Miért nevezik Ábrahámot a hit atyjának?
o: Mert bízott Isten ígéretében akkor is, amikor nem látta a beteljesedést

en.q: Why is Abraham called the father of faith?
o: Because he trusted God's promise even when he could not yet see it fulfilled
Because he was a strong soldier
Because he built a fine house

bio.hu: A testvérei eladták rabszolgának, mégsem keseredett meg. Egyiptomban Isten bölcsességet adott neki, és ő mentette meg az éhínségtől az egész családját. Amikor újra találkoztak, azt mondta: ti rosszat terveztetek, de Isten jóra fordította.
bio.en: His brothers sold him as a slave, yet he did not grow bitter. In Egypt God gave him wisdom, and he saved his whole family from the famine. When they met again he said: you intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.

hu.q: Mit csináltatott Jákób Józsefnek?

en.q: What did Jacob have made for Joseph?

hu.q: Hány éves volt József, amikor a testvérei eladták?

en.q: How old was Joseph when his brothers sold him?

hu.q: Mennyiért adták el Józsefet?

en.q: For how much was Joseph sold?

hu.q: Kinek a házában szolgált József Egyiptomban?

en.q: In whose house did Joseph serve in Egypt?

hu.q: Mit mondott József, amikor rosszra csábították?

en.q: What did Joseph say when he was tempted to do wrong?

hu.q: Mit jelentett a fáraó álmában a hét kövér és hét sovány tehén?
o: Hét bő és hét éhséges évet

en.q: What did the seven fat and seven thin cows mean in Pharaoh’s dream?
o: Seven good years and seven years of famine

hu.q: Hány éves volt József, amikor a fáraó szolgálatába állt?

en.q: How old was Joseph when he entered Pharaoh’s service?

hu.q: Mit mondott József a testvéreinek a végén?
o: „Ti rosszat terveztetek, de Isten jóra fordította.”

en.q: What did Joseph finally say to his brothers?
o: „You intended to harm me, but God intended it for good.”

hu.q: Mit kért József a halála előtt?

en.q: What did Joseph ask for before he died?
o: That they carry his bones with them
That he be buried in Egypt
That they build him a statue
